summary: H.R. 3898, known as the PERMIT Act, amends the Federal Water Pollution Control Act to make targeted reforms to waters of the United States and other matters. The bill redefines navigable waters to exclude certain features, adjusts timelines and procedures for water quality certifications and permits, extends permit terms, and alters rules relating to agricultural stormwater, pesticide discharges, and compensatory mitigation.

affected_groups.effect: Exempts agricultural stormwater discharges from permit requirements and clarifies rules for prior converted croplands and voluntary participation in water quality pilot programs.
Extends permit and general permit durations to 10 years, streamlines nationwide permits for linear and pipeline projects, and sets strict timelines for judicial review of certifications.
Ratifies existing state Clean Water Act Section 404 permit programs (Michigan, New Jersey, Florida) and provides pathways and incentives for additional states to administer programs.
Removes federal and state permit requirements under the Act for the application of authorized pesticides into navigable waters, subject to specific exceptions.

key_provisions: Redefines 'navigable waters' under the Clean Water Act to exclude waste treatment systems, ephemeral features flowing only from precipitation, prior converted cropland, groundwater, and other excluded features.
Extends the maximum term for National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permits from five years to ten years.
Exempts agricultural stormwater discharges and certain pesticide applications from Clean Water Act permit requirements.
Expands nationwide general permits for linear infrastructure projects and linear pipeline projects, and extends general permit terms from five years to ten years.

Establishes strict timelines, standing limitations, and expedited judicial review requirements for water quality certifications and permit decisions, particularly affecting energy transmission facilities.
Ratifies existing state permit programs for dredged or fill material in Michigan, New Jersey, and Florida, and prohibits the EPA from withdrawing approval without congressional authorization.
Directs the Secretary of the Army and the EPA to revise the compensatory mitigation framework for aquatic resource losses, incorporating flexibility and recognizing approved reclamation plans.
missing_information: Specific economic costs or budgetary appropriations associated with implementing the act's various permit reviews, backlog reductions, and reporting requirements are not detailed in the source.
summary_detail.plain_summary: H.R. 3898, known as the PERMIT Act, amends the Federal Water Pollution Control Act to make targeted reforms to waters of the United States and other matters. The bill redefines navigable waters to exclude certain features, adjusts timelines and procedures for water quality certifications and permits, extends permit terms, and alters rules relating to agricultural stormwater, pesticide discharges, and compensatory mitigation.
summary_detail.significance: The PERMIT Act significantly alters federal water pollution control regulations by narrowing the geographic scope of federal jurisdiction over waters, extending permit lengths, and streamlining the approval processes for energy, infrastructure, and agricultural activities.
